turns.text: I remember the day my mother came home shaking, clutching that black sash they forced her to wear. She was seventy years old, and you—people like you—decided she was an enemy because her father owned a bit of land decades ago. You didn’t care that she’d worked her whole life or that her hands were cracked from scrubbing floors. You made her wear that mark, walk through the streets with her head down, as if she was filth. I watched her shrink every day. At dinner, she barely spoke. She stopped singing. My own children saw their grandmother humiliated, and I could not explain to them why the world had turned upside down. The day she left for Hebei, carrying a bundle and that damned sash, I felt something in me break. You did that. Your slogans, your armbands, your shouting—those were the tools that ground my family into dust. Tell me, did you ever look at the old women you dragged out and feel anything but pride?

You want to know if I felt pride. That day, I was standing in the hospital courtyard, sweat running down my back, holding a loudspeaker that made my hands shake. The old women—your mother’s age—were lined up in front of us, sashes around their necks, faces grey and drained. I remember one woman’s hands: swollen knuckles, blue veins, trembling as she tried to hold her sash straight. The crowd jeered, some spat. I yelled slogans, my throat raw, my voice cracking. I felt power in that moment, yes—power I’d never had before, not in school, not at home.

But pride? It’s not so simple. There was a kind of fever in me, a sense that I was finally on the right side, finally someone who mattered. When I looked at those women, I told myself they were symbols, not people. That’s how I kept going, how I shouted at a grandmother until she stumbled and nearly fell. I told myself her suffering was necessary, that history demanded it. But when I saw her later, slumped by the curb, clutching that sash like a lifeline, I felt something twist inside me. I pushed it down. If I’d let myself feel pity, I’d have been next. That’s the truth. I chose to shout louder. I made myself part of the machine. I don’t expect forgiveness. But I remember every face.

You talk about fever and power—how convenient. You could pick up a loudspeaker and turn a trembling grandmother into a symbol, but you never had to pick up the pieces afterward. You didn’t see how, after your “necessary suffering,” my mother’s hands shook so badly she couldn’t hold her chopsticks. You didn’t hear the way my father’s voice went flat, how he stopped looking people in the eye. At work, I was forced to stand with my back against the wall, reading big-character posters denouncing people I’d known for years. I remember my own supervisor, a war veteran, his medals hidden away, head bowed, lips pressed tight, as children half his age screamed in his face. You did that. You made us hide our photographs, tear up old letters, burn anything with a foreign stamp. My son asked why we had to put our books in a sack and bury them in the garden. I lied to him. I lied to my own child, because of your “fever.” Do you know what it’s like to teach your children to be silent, to trust no one, not even their friends? You say you remember every face. I wonder if you remember the silence you left behind.

I remember the silence, yes. It was thick, like fog, after the shouting stopped. I remember standing in a ransacked living room, the air stinking of sweat and fear, papers scattered everywhere—photographs torn, calligraphy scrolls trampled under muddy shoes. We called it “clearing out the old,” but really it was destruction. I watched a woman—she might have been your mother’s age—drop to her knees, clutching a broken frame. I told her to stand up, voice hard, but my own hands were shaking. I told myself I was building something new. I didn’t think about the emptiness left behind.

You talk about hiding medals, burning letters, teaching your children to lie. I saw that, too—my own father, a man who’d been praised for his work, suddenly afraid to look out the window, his voice barely above a whisper. At night, I heard my parents arguing in the kitchen, their words clipped and frantic, worried I’d be next. I knew what I was doing to others. I still went out the next morning, armband tight on my sleeve, because if I hesitated, if I showed doubt, someone would notice. I beat teachers, poured ink on their faces, and watched them cower. I shaved a woman’s head myself, the dull clipper catching and tearing at her scalp, her screams ringing in my ears long after I left the room. I made choices—sometimes out of fear, sometimes out of anger, sometimes because I wanted to belong. I won’t pretend I didn’t. The silence you describe—I carried it home with me, too. Even now, when I hear a sudden shout or see an old photograph, I feel it settle over me again.

You carried it home, you say, but you got to choose when to take off your armband. My son never got to take off his shame. He was marked by what you did, by what you called us, by the way the neighborhood children spat at him and called him “enemy’s seed.” I still remember the day he came home with blood on his shirt, belt marks across his back, and I could do nothing—because if I went to the work unit to complain, we’d all be dragged out next. We ate in silence. We never invited anyone over. Every knock on the door made my heart race. I stopped sleeping through the night. My hands still shake when I hear boots in the stairwell.

You poured ink on teachers’ faces. You shaved women’s heads. You say you were afraid, but you had the choice to be cruel or to step back, even if it cost you. The rest of us had no choice but to endure. You talk about your fear, but it was our lives that were shattered, our families that were scattered, our names that became curses. My mother died in Hebei, alone. I never saw her again. You made a spectacle out of her suffering, and then you went home. Tell me, when you see an old woman on the bus now, do you look away? Or do you still check her family background before you let her sit down?

I don’t check anyone’s background anymore. When I see an old woman on the bus now—hair thin, back bent, hands gripping the seat in front of her—I look at the floor. I can’t meet her eyes. Sometimes I hear a cough or catch a whiff of mothballs and something in me jolts, like I’m sixteen again and standing in a courtyard, shouting myself hoarse while someone’s grandmother tries to disappear into her own shadow.

You say I had a choice. Maybe I did, at least for a moment. I remember one afternoon at No. 110 Middle School, a teacher—she was small, always wore the same faded blue jacket—was hauled up in front of the assembly. The others wanted to pour ink on her head. I hesitated, just for a second. One of the girls—she was always the first to act—shoved the bottle into my hand, eyes daring me to refuse. I poured. The ink ran down her face and she sobbed, shoulders shaking. I felt sick, but I did it. I could have thrown the bottle down and walked away, but I didn’t. I wanted to be safe. I wanted to belong.

You’re right. I went home, washed the ink from my hands, and ate dinner in silence. But that stain never really left. When I see old women now, I see the ones I humiliated, the ones who never came back from the countryside, the ones who hung themselves in the duty room while I was busy guarding the stairwell. I don’t look away because I’m proud—I look away because I’m ashamed. And that shame is something I put on myself, every single day, like an armband I can’t take off.
